title: Supervised learning & the standard workflow
intro: Supervised learning = learning from input-output pairs (X, y), plus the fixed fit→predict→score steps you always follow in scikit-learn.
keyPoints: Supervised learning = learning from labelled examples (X with y).
The fixed scikit-learn order: import → instantiate → fit → predict → score.
Trust only the test score — the train score says nothing about new data.

blocks.html: Supervised learning learns a mapping from inputs X (features) to outputs y (targets) from examples. Classification predicts categories, regression continuous numbers. This course: classification with the two most popular linear classifiers — logistic regression and SVMs.
Supervised learning = learning from examples of input-output pairs (X, y), so that you can predict the correct output for new input.

sections.title: The scikit-learn workflow: fit → predict → score

blocks.html: Four fixed steps for every model: import, instantiate (set hyperparameters), fit with fit(X, y), and predict/evaluate with predict or score. A hyperparameter is a choice made before fitting that steers complexity.

blocks.caption: The complete workflow with KNN on the digits dataset
blocks.source:
from sklearn.datasets import load_digits
from sklearn.neighbors import KNeighborsClassifier

# 1. Load the data: X = images (8x8 pixels), y = digit 0-9
X, y = load_digits(return_X_y=True)
print('X shape:', X.shape, '| y shape:', y.shape)

# 2. Instantiate + set hyperparameters
knn = KNeighborsClassifier(n_neighbors=5)

# 3. Fit on the training data
knn.fit(X, y)

# 4. Predict and score
y_pred = knn.predict(X)
print('First 5 predictions:', y_pred[:5])
print('True digits        :', y[:5])
print('Training score     :', round(knn.score(X, y), 3))

blocks.html: y_pred contains one prediction per row of X — even when you call predict on the training data itself, as above.

sections.title: Generalising: why a test score is mandatory

blocks.html: A ~100% training score says little. Hold out 25% with train_test_split, refit on the training set and evaluate on the test set: only then do you measure generalization. In the course KNN drops from ~100% (train) to ~66% (test) on newsgroups data.

blocks.label: accuracy
blocks.caption: The score function of scikit-learn classifiers computes accuracy by default.
Honest evaluation with train_test_split
blocks.source:
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split

X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(
    X, y, test_size=0.25, random_state=42)

# Fit ONLY on the training set
knn = KNeighborsClassifier(n_neighbors=5)
knn.fit(X_train, y_train)

print('Train score:', round(knn.score(X_train, y_train), 3))
print('Test score :', round(knn.score(X_test,  y_test), 3))

blocks.html: Never train on the test set. The test set is a "simulation" of new data — as soon as the model sees it during fitting, you are no longer measuring generalisation but memorisation.
